papers.title: Seizure-like behaviors in a mutant mouse with increased calpain-dependent cleavage of αII-spectrin.
papers.abstract: Mutations inSPTAN1, the gene encoding the neuronal cytoskeletal protein αII-spectrin, are associated with epilepsy and movement disorders, complicating the clinical interpretation of seizure-like behaviors. Stress-induced paroxysmal motor events can mimic behaviors typically observed in epileptic seizures, yet they do not exhibit definitive electrophysiological correlates. This study investigated the link between seizure-like behaviors and the brain's cortical electroencephalographic (EEG) activity in heterozygousSptan1R1098Q mice, a novel model of spectrin-related neurodevelopmental disease. Mutant and wild-type (WT) mice were subject to automated gait analysis, long-term video-EEG monitoring, and a handling-induced seizure susceptibility (HISS) paradigm at various ages. R1098Q mice demonstrated pronounced gait abnormalities characteristic of ataxia as well as age-related increases in delta and theta power, and spike-wave discharges (SWD), suggesting elevated network excitability. During the HISS test, nearly all mutant mice exhibited significant seizure-like motor responses, such as forelimb clonus, impaired balance, and falls, whereas WT mice displayed no abnormal reactions. Notably, these motor behaviors did not coincide with cortical ictal EEG activity. Rather, stress induced a transient suppression of cortical EEG spiking, followed by the return of interictal spiking and SWDs. The present findings demonstrate a dissociation between seizure-like behaviors and cortical ictal EEG activity inSptan1R1098Q mice. These findings emphasize the limitations inherent to classifying seizures based solely on behavioral observations and underscore the necessity of incorporating electrophysiological data when evaluating seizure-like manifestations in genetic epilepsy models characterized by significant motor dysfunction. Such differentiation holds substantial relevance for preclinical epilepsy research and informs the interpretation of seizure-like events within neurogenetic disorders.

papers.title: Lifestyle profiles and trajectories of intrinsic capacity: Longitudinal data from the INSPIRE-T study.
papers.abstract: Intrinsic capacity (IC), a pillar of healthy ageing, may be influenced by lifestyle behaviours. We evaluated associations between lifestyle profiles and IC trajectories. In this longitudinal study, 656 participants (63% female; age 20-100 years) from the INSPIRE-T cohort with complete lifestyle and IC data were included. Age-adjusted lifestyle profiles were identified using Latent Profile Analysis based on dietary patterns (DPs) (Plant-based, ultra-processed foods-associated [UPF-associate], Mediterranean [MDS], or DASH), leisure-time and transportation physical activity (LTPA), sedentary time, and sleep quality. IC scores derived from cognition, locomotion, psychology, vitality, and sensory domains were classified according to age- and sex-standardised IC centiles at baseline and 3-year follow-up (the number of participants contributing data varied across visits). Linear mixed-effects models examined associations between lifestyle profiles and IC centile trajectories. We identified 13 lifestyle profiles when switching between the 4 DPs (3 for Plant-based, MDS, and DASH, and 4 for UPF-associated). A profile characterised by low LTPA, low intake of the Plant-based DP, high sedentary time, and poor sleep quality was associated with 8 percentile points lower IC at baseline than a profile with a similar diet and sleep pattern, but with higher LTPA and lower sedentary behaviour (β: -8.20, 95%CI: -12.79; -3.60). Furthermore, a profile of low LTPA, high scores for UPF-associated DP, high sedentary time, and poor sleep quality was associated with 11 percentile points lower IC at baseline than a profile in which the quality of sleep was better and the intake of an UPF-associated DP was lower (β: -11.08, 95%CI: -16.44; -5.71). No longitudinal associations were observed. Lifestyle profiles with higher LTPA, low sedentary behaviour, low intake of an UPF-associated diet, and better sleep quality were cross-sectionally associated with better IC.

papers.title: Periodic generalized nonepileptiform discharges (PGNDs) during NREM sleep before nocturnal seizures in temporal and extratemporal lobe epilepsy: An exploratory quantitative EEG study.
papers.abstract: To explore whether the spectral power of periodic generalized nonepileptiform discharges (PGNDs), a newly operationalized subset of CAP A-like NREM slow-wave events, differs between temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) and extratemporal lobe epilepsy (ETLE), and to identify demographic, clinical, and etiological factors associated with delta power. We retrospectively analyzed drug-resistant focal epilepsy patients undergoing long-term video-EEG monitoring (2018-2024) with at least two PGNDs in the preictal period of nocturnal seizures. PGNDs were visually scored and subtyped, and matched interictal NREM controls were selected. Absolute and relative (amplitude-normalized) spectral power was calculated for five frequency bands. Analyses were performed at the patient level, with false discovery rate (FDR) correction, cross-validated ROC analysis, confounder-adjusted models, and a mixed-effects model for determinants of delta power. Sixty-eight patients (35 TLE, 33 ETLE; 124 seizures, 711 PGNDs) met inclusion criteria. Delta (0.5-2.4 Hz) power of the PGND just before seizure onset (PGND1) was higher in ETLE than TLE, both in absolute terms (p = 0.016) and relative to total power (51.6% vs. 45.1%, p = 0.006, FDR q = 0.035), and the difference persisted after adjustment for carbamazepine use. Discrimination was modest (AUC=0.669; leave-one-out sensitivity 61%, specificity 74%). Absolute electrode-level differences did not survive FDR correction, whereas relative PGND1 delta power remained higher in ETLE at 16 of 20 electrodes after correction, indicating a widespread rather than regional difference. No within-patient preictal increase in PGND power was observed. Only febrile seizure history was independently associated with delta power. PGND delta power differs between ETLE and TLE independently of overall EEG amplitude, suggesting localization-related differences in NREM slow-wave events rather than a preictal biomarker. Given the modest discrimination and exploratory design, validation in independent cohorts is required before any clinical application.

papers.title: Mandibular advancement device vs continuous positive airway pressure in obstructive sleep apnea: An updated systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common sleep-related breathing disorder that increases the risk of cardiovascular diseases. While continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) remains the first-line therapy for OSA, adherence continues to be a major challenge. Recently, mandibular advancement devices (MADs) have emerged as a safe and effective alternative. This systematic review and meta-analysis aim to compare MAD and CPAP across several health outcomes. Following PRISMA guidelines, six databases were searched, and the protocol was preregistered on PROSPERO (CRD420251081182). Primary outcomes included apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), minimum peripheral capillary oxygen saturation (SpO2), oxygen desaturation index (ODI), and several blood pressure (BP) parameters. Secondary outcomes included adherence, BMI, among others. A meta-analysis was performed using R version 4.6.0 and heterogeneity was assessed using I2 statistics. A total of 18 studies were included with 1244 participants. The CPAP group showed improvement in SpO2 (MD = -4.54, 95% CI: -5.50 to -3.59; p < 0.01; I2 = 50.2%), ODI (MD = 6.54, 95% CI: 3.70 to 9.38; p < 0.01; I2 = 85.4%), and arousal index (MD = 4.40, 95% CI: 1.22 to 7.58; p = <0.01; I2 = 77.5%). The MAD group showed significantly greater adherence (MD = 1.43, 95% CI: 1.10 to 1.77; p < 0.01; I2 = 55.6%) and modest significant reduction in several BP parameters. Meta-regression identified baseline AHI as a significant moderator of treatment effect (β = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.30 to 1.35; p < 0.01). This review suggests that treatment selection between CPAP and MAD may be informed by OSA severity and expected adherence. CPAP remains superior in improving polysomnographic parameters. Further long-term trials incorporating objectively monitored adherence and hard cardiovascular outcomes are needed to guide individualized treatment selection in OSA.

papers.title: When Is Circadian Resetting Adaptive? Comment on "Chrono-mechanobiology: The complex interactions between mechanotransduction and circadian rhythms in the intervertebral disc and articular cartilage, in health and disease" by Zerihun G. Workineh et al.
Lewis ladder: A web application that draws ladder diagrams from the surface electrocardiogram.
papers.abstract: Ladder diagrams represent proposed arrhythmic activation sequences, but they are still drawn by hand, and the intracardiac recording that each diagram predicts is rarely made explicit. No available tool derives the diagram from intervals measured on the patient's own tracing. Lewis Ladder is a free web application for teaching surface electrocardiographic interpretation with ladder diagrams. The user marks P-wave and QRS onsets on a calibrated strip; the engine measures the intervals, applies 11 exclusion and 24 caution rules taken from published electrophysiologic criteria to 14 candidate readings, and draws the ladder diagram of each reading that remains, including paced rhythms. All rules, thresholds, and assumed conduction times are tabulated. On 28 synthetic tracings of known mechanism, the intended reading was never excluded, with exact marks or with every mark displaced by random error (standard deviation up to 20 ms; 11,200 classifications), and 794 automated checks cover the engine. A free-drawing mode supports diagrams built by hand. Two schematic extensions, an electrophysiology view of the implied intracardiac channels and a network model of conduction that the user can pace, are proofs of concept. The application is a teaching aid that makes mechanistic hypotheses explicit and checkable against the tracing. It is not a diagnostic device. Educational benefit has not been measured, and the schematic electrograms have been checked only against published sources. Onsets and QRS duration are entered manually, and the network model does not reproduce every pacing response observed during catheter studies.

papers.title: Dupilumab for Moderate-to-Severe Chronic Prurigo Nodularis: A Retrospective Real-World Study of Effectiveness, Safety, and Prolonged Dosing Intervals.
papers.abstract: Chronic prurigo nodularis (CPN) is a multidimensional neuro-immunocutaneous disease characterized by severe, persistent pruritus, and the development of nodular lesions caused by repeated scratching, often associated with sleep disruption, psychological distress, and impaired quality of life. Dupilumab has demonstrated efficacy and safety in clinical trials, but evidence regarding the use of prolonged dosing intervals, and potential modifiers of response in real-world settings remains limited. We conducted a single-center, retrospective, observational study of adults with moderate-to-severe CPN treated with dupilumab in routine clinical practice. The primary endpoint was clinically meaningful pruritus improvement at week 24, defined as a ≥ 4-point reduction in Worst Itch-Numeric Rating Scale (WI-NRS). Secondary outcomes included achievement of Investigator's Global Assessment for Prurigo Nodularis-Stage (IGA PN-S) 0/1 and longitudinal changes in pruritus, nodular lesion burden, sleep disturbance, and quality of life. Adverse events, treatment discontinuation, exploratory baseline predictors of response, and patterns of dosing-interval extension and return to the standard every-2-week regimen were also recorded. In total, 26 patients were included. Median age at dupilumab initiation was 45.5 years (interquartile range [IQR] 33-53 years), and median follow-up was 50 weeks (IQR 32-62 years). Baseline disease burden was substantial, with severe itch, marked quality-of-life impairment, sleep disturbance, elevated impulsivity scores, and psychiatric comorbidity in 19 patients (73%). At week 24, 59% of patients achieved a ≥ 4-point WI-NRS reduction, while 45% achieved IGA PN-S 0/1 and combined WI-NRS-IGA PN-S response. A sustained improvement in itch, clinical severity, and quality of life was observed among evaluable patients through later follow-up. Prolongation of the dupilumab dosing interval was attempted in nine controlled responders and maintained without return to the standard regimen in five patients. Psychiatric comorbidity was associated with lower odds of WI-NRS response at week 24. Adverse events occurred in two patients (7.7%) and led to treatment withdrawal in one owing to gastrointestinal disorder. Dupilumab showed real-world effectiveness and a favorable safety profile in moderate-to-severe CPN. These findings support individualized, multidisciplinary management and further prospective investigation of response predictors and dosing-interval prolongation strategies. Graphical Abstract available for this article. Chronic prurigo nodularis (CPN) is a long-lasting skin disease that causes very intense itching and hard itchy bumps. Scratching can keep the disease going, and many people also have sleep problems, emotional distress, and a major effect on daily life. Dupilumab is an injectable treatment that blocks two immune signals involved in inflammation and itch. Clinical trials have shown that dupilumab can help people with this disease, but less is known about how patients treated in everyday clinical practice will respond. In this study, we reviewed the medical records of 26 adults with moderate-to-severe CPN treated with dupilumab. After 24 weeks, 59% of patients who could be assessed had a meaningful reduction in worst itch, and in 45% the skin disease was clear or almost clear according to the doctor's assessment. Improvements in itch, skin signs, and quality of life generally continued during later follow-up. Overall, nine patients with good disease control were able to receive dupilumab less often; however, four needed to return to the standard every-2-week schedule. Side effects were uncommon and led to stopping treatment in one patient. Patients with mental health conditions seemed less likely to have a strong itch response, but this finding needs confirmation. These results support care that is tailored to each person, including mental health support when needed.

papers.title: Refractive status and visual function in patients with pre-presbyopia and presbyopia wearing monofocal soft contact lenses without glasses in daily life.
papers.abstract: To investigate the refractive status and visual function of patients with pre-presbyopia and presbyopia using monofocal soft contact lenses (CLs) without glasses in daily life. Cross-sectional observational study METHODS: We included 102 participants wearing monofocal soft CLs without glasses. They underwent ocular measurements of distant and near visual acuity (DVA and NVA, respectively), accommodative amplitude, and maximal and minimal pupillary diameters. Further, they completed the Near Activity Visual Questionnaire (NAVQ), Contact Lens Dry Eye Questionnaire, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, and Subjective Happiness Scale. Over 80% of participants maintained DVA and NVA of 0.0 logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution or better in their 40s; however, the NVA declined sharply in their 50s. Subjective refraction with CLs became more myopic with age, with a greater decline in the more myopic eye, which led to increased interocular differences. Risk factors for undercorrection included older age and female sex. The NAVQ scores and difference in pupillary diameter showed a non-significant negative correlation with undercorrection. Patients with presbyopia wearing monofocal CLs showed significant declines in NVA and DVA in their 50s, with trends toward undercorrection, possibly to compensate for near visual impairment. Age, sex, and pupillary dynamics should be considered when optimising refractive correction.

Environmental noise and cardiometabolic health: a transatlantic perspective.
papers.abstract: Environmental noise is a pervasive but under-recognized cardiovascular and metabolic risk factor. Drawing on prior expert reviews and large-scale epidemiologic and mechanistic studies, this review synthesizes evidence on the burden, major clinical associations, biological pathways, vulnerable populations, and mitigation strategies relevant to cardiovascular health. Road traffic noise is consistently and dose-dependently associated with higher risks of ischaemic heart disease, stroke, heart failure, diabetes, sleep disturbance, and adverse mental health outcomes, whereas for railway and aircraft noise, the evidence base is less consistent, although important associations are increasingly reported. Translational human imaging studies, controlled exposure experiments, and animal models converge on a common pathway in which chronic and intermittent noise exposure activates stress-responsive neural circuits, increases sympathetic and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activity, promotes oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and vascular inflammation, and may thereby accelerate cardiometabolic disease. Noise frequently co-occurs with air pollution, heat, and adverse social and built environments, particularly in socioeconomically disadvantaged communities, and these combined exposures may contribute additively to cardiovascular risk. These effects are especially relevant in urban populations with nighttime exposure and multiple co-exposures. Despite this growing evidence base, environmental noise remains largely absent from contemporary cardiovascular risk assessment tools, prevention guidelines, and routine patient counselling, representing a missed opportunity for risk reduction. Effective mitigation will require a hierarchical strategy combining source reduction, health-informed urban and transport planning, and targeted individual protection. Reducing environmental noise exposure should be recognized as an important opportunity to protect and advance cardiovascular and metabolic health in the 21st century.

papers.title: TToTP model: An automated detection of Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia using Tesla Tree of Thought Pattern with EEG signals.
papers.abstract: BackgroundAlzheimer's disease (AD) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are common neurological disorders.Objective:To facilitate the early detection of these conditions, we aimed to propose a new self-organized explainable feature engineering (SOXFE) model. Additionally, we sought to investigate the feature extraction capabilities.MethodsWe used a publicly available electroencephalography (EEG) dementia detection dataset. This dataset was created to collect EEG signals from participants in three categories: (i) AD, (ii) FTD, and (iii) healthy control (HC). To automatically detect these groups, we proposed a new SOXFE model. This model includes a novel feature extraction function inspired by Tesla's 369 vortex and the Tree of Thought (ToT), termed the Tesla Tree of Thought Pattern (TToTP). In the feature selection phase, we applied cumulative weighted iterative neighborhood component analysis (CWINCA), to select the most informative features. In the classification phase, we employed the t algorithm-based k-nearest neighbors (tkNN). The fourth phase involves information fusion, where the results from each channel are voted on using iterative majority voting (IMV), and the best outcome is selected. The final phase is explainable results generation, in which a cortical channel map (CCMap) is created based on the findings from the information fusion phase.ResultsWe applied the TToTP-based SOXFE model to the EEG dementia dataset, achieving over 99% classification accuracy. Additionally, a cortical channel map was generated using the classification results.ConclusionsThe proposed TToTP-based SOXFE model achieved high classification performance and successfully generated a cortical channel map. The model contributes to both feature engineering and neuroscience.

papers.title: Pharmacological and non-pharmacological management of sleep disturbances in Alzheimer's disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: BackgroundSleep disturbances affect half of Alzheimer's disease patients, accelerating cognitive decline and increasing caregiver burden. The comparative effectiveness of available interventions remains unclear.ObjectiveTo compare pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions on sleep outcomes in Alzheimer's disease using network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs).MethodsFollowing PRISMA and a registered PROSPERO protocol (CRD420250653178), four databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus, Web of Science) were searched through July 2026 for RCTs. Pairwise and frequentist random-effects network meta-analyses using Hedges' g were performed for six sleep outcomes: total sleep time (TST), wake after sleep onset (WASO), nocturnal awakenings (NoA), sleep efficiency, daytime sleep, and daytime naps. A Bayesian network meta-analysis served as a sensitivity analysis.ResultsTwelve RCTs (N = 936, 32 study arms) were included. Zolpidem and zopiclone reduced sleep fragmentation, with improvements in NoA (SMD -1.09) and WASO (SMD -0.86), although these findings were based on a single short-term trial. Suvorexant increased TST (SMD 0.376) and increased TST (SMD 0.376), while lemborexant 2.5 mg reduced NoA (SMD -0.98), with favorable short-term tolerability. Walking (SMD -0.48), bright light therapy (SMD -0.37), and NITE-AD (SMD -0.52) reduced NoA, while combined light therapy and melatonin reduced daytime sleep (SMD -0.858). Melatonin monotherapy, trazodone, and mirtazapine showed limited or inconsistent effects.ConclusionsNon-pharmacological interventions may be considered before pharmacological treatment. When pharmacotherapy is required, dual orexin receptor antagonists may be useful for selected sleep outcomes, whereas Z-drugs should be used cautiously given their established safety concerns. Larger, longer-duration head-to-head trials using standardized sleep outcomes are needed.

papers.title: An occupational medicine perspective; lessons from an Arctic research settlement.
papers.abstract: This occupational health risk assessment was undertaken in the austere high Arctic Ny Alesund Research Station, the most northerly permanent settlement on the globe, and explores the occupational health impacts seen in this extreme environment. The community hosts researchers from a vast array of subject areas, such as ecology, glaciology, oceanography and astrophysics. This study took the form of a workplace health risk assessment using both qualitative and quantitative assessment methods, such as observational walk-through surveys and environmental measurements, including ambient temperature, wind speed and UV levels. The assessment identified potential circadian rhythm disruption by polar nights and midnight sun, UV-associated skin cancer and sunburn, cataracts, musculoskeletal strain/injury and thermal injury as key health risks. Polar bears, marine life, snowmobile and powerboat use, and climbing and traversing 55% of the glacier cover present a special hazard profile. A focus on communication and relationships, increased exercise levels, reduced screen time, and reduced air pollution may be seen as potential benefits. There are knowledge gaps highlighted which require further study in terms of the long-term health effects of persistent organic pollutants and of repeated cold exposure, as well as how to manage medically vulnerable cold-exposed workers from an occupational health perspective.

papers.title: Burnout, Lack of Sleep and the Resulting Reduced Clinical Performance of Neurologists are a Global Problem.
Novel antimicrobial pyrimidin-2-one (thione) azo disperse dyes for polyester fabrics.
papers.abstract: The present study involves the synthesis of a new series of pyrimidinone (thione) azo dyes (3a-6d). The structure of these compounds was elucidated by elemental and spectral analysis. The multifunctional dyeing performance of these dyes on polyester was systematically evaluated in terms of color strength, dyeing time, concentration, pH, exhaustion, and fastness properties. Colorimetric measurements and fastness tests gave satisfactory results, confirming the suitability of these dyes for polyester fabrics. The antimicrobial evaluation revealed structure-dependent activity profiles against S. epidermidis, S. haemolyticus, P. aeruginosa, K. pneumoniae, and C. albicans. Schiff bases 2a, b showed modest activity only against Gram-positive strains, while azo linkage introduction expanded the antimicrobial spectrum. Compounds 4a, b emerged as the most potent agents against multidrug-resistant S. haemolyticus (27.5 mm), K. pneumoniae (21.0 mm), and C. albicans (27.3 mm), despite 90.9-100% resistance to conventional antibiotics. Compounds 5a, b and 6a-d showed negligible activity, except weak antifungal effects for 6a. Cytotoxicity assessment against WISH normal cells revealed moderate-to-weak toxicity (IC50 = 42.65-92.39 µM) for most compounds, with 6c being the least cytotoxic member of the series (IC50 > 100 µM, non-cytotoxic), although it produced no detectable inhibition zone against any organism in the panel. The most potent antimicrobials 4a, b displayed moderate-to-strong cytotoxicity (IC50 = 23.04 and 19.46 µM) but were less cytotoxic than doxorubicin (8.72 µM) and sorafenib (13.45 µM). Collectively, 4a, b are promising dual-action antimicrobial leads against multidrug-resistant pathogens, while 6c was non-cytotoxic and is of interest only as a starting framework for further optimization.

papers.title: Collapse of local circuit integrated information Φ during NREM sleep.
papers.abstract: Clarifying the mechanisms underlying the emergence of consciousness remains a fundamental challenge in modern neuroscience. Integrated Information Theory (IIT) provides a mathematical framework derived from the phenomenological properties of consciousness as its axioms. IIT proposes that consciousness is identical to a system's intrinsic cause-effect information structure, quantified by integrated information Φ. While IIT predicts that the Φ of a neuronal system should decrease during the loss of consciousness, this hypothesis has remained untested at the neural circuit level. The present study provides empirical support for this IIT prediction. It was found that Φ within local circuits decreases during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep compared to wakefulness (and REM sleep in the frontal cortex), regardless of cortical laminar structure. The reduction in Φ was particularly pronounced during OFF-periods, when neural activity is collectively suppressed. These results align with IIT's framework, suggesting that the loss of consciousness corresponds to a collapse of integrated information within local circuits. The findings provide empirical support for IIT as a mathematical theory aiming to explain conscious experiences.

papers.title: Electromagnetic field theories of conscious experience: a conceptual review and reappraisal.
papers.abstract: This paper reviews and contrasts electromagnetic field (EMF) theories of consciousness with traditional neural and functionalist accounts of phenomenal space and its contents. Conscious experience is unified yet differentiated, intentional, reportable, and capable of influencing behaviour. These properties, available only from a first-person perspective, must correspond to distinct states or processes in an underlying physical substrate. Conventional neural and functionalist theories explain conscious experience through local causal interactions among discrete units and symbolic processing. However, patterns of computation and causal organization exist only from an external observer's perspective and therefore do not themselves explain subjective experience. In contrast, the brain's endogenous EMF, which integrates information spatially, provides a plausible substrate for phenomenal unity. Evidence linking EMF dynamics to conscious states and contents is abundant, particularly from EEG studies showing reliable correlations despite attenuation of extracranial fields. EMF dynamics may also provide a more stable representation of short-term memory than variable neural firing patterns. Evidence for ephaptic coupling further demonstrates that EMFs influence neural activity, potentially contributing to rapid large-scale neural coordination and fluctuations in firing thresholds. Experimental perturbation of endogenous EMFs can alter conscious experience and modulate oscillations involved in memory consolidation. EMFs can perform field computation through superposition, and a gradual evolutionary origin follows from the adaptive advantages of ephaptic coupling in simpler nervous systems. It is hypothesized that low-frequency oscillations provide the basis of phenomenal space, whereas localized high-frequency oscillations support experiential differentiation. Intentionality is explained by locating the conscious EMF between sensory input and motor output processes.

papers.title: Childhood and adolescent changes in sleep spindle trends across the night.
papers.abstract: Sleep spindle trends across sleep cycles provide clues to factors that influence these distinct EEG waveforms. We describe cycle trends in spindle density, frequency, amplitude, and duration, and we determine how these trends change across childhood and adolescence. Furthermore, we test how the trends in spindle density are related to trends in slow wave (delta) EEG incidence. A computer program detected and measured sleep spindles in central and frontal EEG from 1944 nights from our longitudinal dataset of semiannual recordings from 97 participants, ages 6-18 years. Spindle density and duration increased steeply between cycles 1 and 2 with smaller increases across subsequent cycles. The magnitude of these increases decreased with age. The spindle density cycle trend was strongly related to the delta cycle trend, but the age-related change in the density trend was not related to changes in delta. Spindle wave frequency shifted from an increase across cycles in children to a u-shaped trend in older adolescents, whereas central spindle amplitude shifted from a u-shaped trend to a linear increase. The trends in frontal and central spindles were, on the whole, similar with exceptions suggesting later maturation of frontal circuits. The age-related changes in sleep spindle measures across sleep cycles cannot be attributed solely to thalamocortical pruning but must also be affected by myelination and circuit reorganization. The age-related changes in cycle trends for spindle frequency indicate a shift from a strong homeostatic influence in children to greater circadian influence in late adolescence.

papers.title: Social bilingual language use is associated with neural efficiency in inhibitory control: Evidence from ERPs.
papers.abstract: Cognitive control supports flexible goal maintenance and conflict resolution. Although bilingual experience has been proposed to enhance its efficiency through sustained language control, emerging evidence suggests these effects reflect adaptive recalibration driven by individual language use rather than domain-general transfer. Here we examined how individual differences in bilingual experience modulate behavioral and neural indices of adaptive attentional control during conflict processing, as indexed by an adaptive Flanker task. Fifty participants (M = 19.6 years) completed the Language and Social Background Questionnaire and an electroencephalography adaptive Flanker task. Event-related potentials in the N100, N200 and P300 windows indexed attentional allocation, conflict detection, and monitoring. Behaviorally, participants showed the expected Flanker interference effect, with no modulation by bilingual experience. In contrast, greater Non-English Social Use, but not overall bilingualism or home use, was associated with attenuated N100s and N200s, suggesting reduced early attentional demands. These neural effects, in the absence of behavioral differences, suggest experience-dependent efficiency in control recruitment rather than enhanced control.

papers.title: Sleep, An Evolving Process: Exploring the Experience, Needs, and Help-Seeking Behavior of Individuals with Spinal Cord Injuries Experiencing Sleep Disturbances.
papers.abstract: People with spinal cord injuries (SCI) often experience poor sleep, impacting their emotional well-being and quality of life, yet sleep disturbances are frequently unmanaged and associated help-seeking behavior is not well understood. This study explores (1) lived experiences of sleep disturbance post SCI and (2) help-seeking behaviors, including support accessed or reasons for not seeking help. This was a qualitative study conducted in a community setting in Queensland, Australia. Semi-structured individual interviews were conducted online between March and June 2025 with 12 people with SCI (66.8% male; 30-64 years old) who experienced self-reported sleep disturbances. The interviews were thematically analyzed using Ritchie and Spencer's 5-step framework method employing a hybrid deductive-inductive approach. Thematic analysis identified 3 themes. Theme 1 (Identifying sleep as a problem) depicts the challenges of recognizing sleep as an issue, given the complexity of secondary conditions. Theme 2 (Seeking support for sleep problems) reflects the obstacles to seeking assistance for sleep disturbances from health professionals, leading to self-directed solutions. Theme 3 (Identifying solutions for sleep problems) describes participants' recommendations for sleep support interventions, including early and routine assessments, as well as educational resources for people with SCI and health professionals. People with SCI rely on self-initiated strategies for sleep management, reflecting gaps in clinical expertise in SCI-related sleep issues. Increasing awareness among people with SCI and health professionals about the impacts, causes, and treatable nature of sleep disturbances is essential, alongside further exploration of the solutions identified by participants.

papers.title: Perceptions of Exoskeleton Use During Inpatient Rehabilitation After Spinal Cord Injury: A Mixed-Method Study.
papers.abstract: Overground robotic exoskeletons (OREs) are increasingly integrated into inpatient rehabilitation for individuals with spinal cord injury (SCI), yet limited research exists on the perspectives of both therapists and patients regarding their use. This study aimed to explore the guiding principles therapists use in their practice with ORE and associated perspectives of therapists and patients alike within an inpatient rehabilitation setting. A convergent mixed-methods design was employed. Three one-time questionnaires were administered: a clinical decision-making questionnaire to ORE-trained physical therapists (n = 7), and therapist/patient exoskeleton questionnaires to therapists (n = 8) and patients with incomplete SCI (n = 68). Questionnaires included both quantitative and qualitative components to assess goals, perceived benefits, and challenges and limitations associated with ORE training. Therapists' goals for ORE use varied according to injury severity and generally aligned with perceived physical and psychosocial benefits. Both therapists and patients reported improvements in mobility and emotional well-being. However, agreement on secondary health benefits (e.g., spasticity, sleep, bowel function) was lower. Notably, fear of falling emerged as a concern among patients but was not reported by therapists. Additionally, therapists may need to manage patients' unrealistic expectations towards ORE. Decisions for ORE use were often influenced by patient readiness and rehabilitation goals, often combining traditional therapies along with ORE training. Overall, ORE training is perceived as beneficial in both physical and psychosocial domains by therapists and patients. Effective use requires individualized prescription, expectation management, and consideration of patient-specific goals.
