papers.title: What are the Factors Associated with in-Hospital Sleep Quality in Patients Undergoing Spine Surgery?
papers.abstract: The incidence of sleep disturbances is high in patients undergoing spine surgery. However, the factors associated with sleep quality for these patients are still poorly understood. We conducted a prospective observational cohort study in a spinal surgery ward of referral centre hospital in China. The primary outcome was sleep quality during hospitalization measured with two methods: subjective sleep quality, measured with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index questionnaire (PSQI), and objective sleep quality, measured by a consumer-wearable actigraphy device. Linear regression and logistic regression models were used to explore the factors related to subjective sleep quality, while a multilevel mixed-effects model was used to explore the factors associated with objective sleep quality. 185 patients were included, of whom 184 completed the PSQI. 42.4% patients experienced sleep disturbances with mean PSQI after surgery 7.37 (SD 3.36). Being divorced (-2.30, [95%CI=-4.42 to -0.18], p=0.033), caffeine consumption (-1.74, [95%CI=-3.11 to -0.37], p=0.013), history of sleep disturbance (1.18, [95%CI=0.23 to 2.13], p=0.016), pain (0.40, [95%CI=0.03 to 0.78], p=0.035) and depression (0.16, [95%CI=0.01 to 0.31], p=0.034) were associated factors of subjective postoperative sleep quality and disturbances. Associated factors of objective postoperative sleep quality included age (-0.34, [95%CI=-0.58 to -0.09], p=0.006), preoperative night sleep quality (0.21, [95%CI=0.03 to 0.39], p=0.022) and postoperative time (T4-T7, p<0.001). Age, marital status, history of disturbances, previous sleep quality, consumption of caffeine, depression, pain and postoperative time are associated with the sleep quality of patients undergoing spine surgery. Future interventions to improve sleep quality in these patients should be developed to improve psychological status and pain.

papers.title: Circadian Disruption and Chrono-rehabilitation After Spinal Cord Injury.
papers.abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) disrupts circadian biology through multiple mechanisms, including dysregulation of core clock genes, inversion of melatonin secretion rhythms, blunted thermoregulatory oscillations, and loss of autonomic pathways that relay timing signals from the suprachiasmatic nucleus to peripheral tissues. These disruptions affect the processes on which rehabilitation depends, that is, neuroplasticity, motor learning consolidation, inflammatory modulation, and tissue repair. Despite this, circadian assessment and intervention remain absent from standard SCI rehabilitation protocols. It can be argued that restoring temporal organization is not ancillary to SCI rehabilitation but is a prerequisite for optimizing functional recovery. However, the evidence underpinning many of the proposed interventions is largely derived from non-SCI populations or preclinical models, and direct clinical trial data in SCI rehabilitation remain limited. Herein, the authors propose a chronobiological framework for SCI rehabilitation that includes systematic sleep-wake assessment using actigraphy and validated questionnaires, timed bright light therapy, individually dosed melatonin supplementation, and scheduling of intensive therapy sessions during patients' peak neurocognitive and motor performance windows. The integration of circadian medicine into SCI rehabilitation requires a shift in perspective; patients are not temporally neutral and their recovery potential is modulated by circadian function.
papers.journal: Topics in spinal cord injury rehabilitation

papers.title: Transformer-based EEG source imaging localizes pathological high-frequency oscillations in focal epilepsy.
papers.abstract: High-frequency oscillations are specific biomarkers of the epileptogenic zone, yet their non-invasive localization from scalp EEG remains challenging due to their brief duration, low amplitude and poor signal-to-noise ratio. Here, we introduce a transformer-based high-frequency oscillation deep source-imaging framework (TH-DeepSIF) trained on biologically realistic neural mass model simulations for non-invasive high-frequency oscillation source imaging. The model was evaluated in simulated single- and dual-source scenarios, where it recovered both the spatial location and temporal dynamics of high-frequency oscillation generators under increasing spatiotemporal complexity. We further validated TH-DeepSIF in 20 patients with drug-resistant epilepsy by comparing reconstructed high-frequency oscillation sources with surgical resection regions. TH-DeepSIF achieved accurate localization and waveform reconstruction in simulations, demonstrating low localization error and strong temporal correspondence with ground truth. In clinical data, pathological high-frequency oscillations (spike ripples) showed strong agreement with resection regions, with a median localization error of 10.9 mm and specificity of 0.883. In a subset of six patients with intracranial EEG, pathological high-frequency oscillation source estimates were spatially close to the seizure onset zone (median localization error: 2.41 mm). Compared with all detected high-frequency oscillations, imaging based on pathological high-frequency oscillations yielded significantly improved spatial correspondence and performance across multiple metrics. Reconstructed source activity was also temporally aligned with both scalp high-frequency oscillation bursts and associated spike deflections. These results demonstrate that TH-DeepSIF provides a data-driven framework for non-invasive high-frequency oscillation source imaging with improved anatomical specificity and support the use of pathological high-frequency oscillations as informative biomarkers for epileptogenic zone localization.

papers.title: Innate Immune Activation as a Shared BMI-Independent Pathway Linking Polycystic Ovary Syndrome and Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Distinct Myeloid Signatures and Suggestive Genetic Signals for EIF2AK2.
papers.abstract: Women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) exhibit a much higher prevalence of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) compared with those without PCOS. Moreover, PCOS women with OSA present poorer metabolic profiles, higher BMI, and greater psychiatric burden. In addition, OSA overlaps with PCOS in its associated comorbidity spectrum. Given that, shared elements were assumed underpin the pathogenesis of PCOS and OSA. Data from the UK Biobank and Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) databases were integrated and analyzed using bioinformatic approaches, single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) analysis, PCA, Firth's penalized logistic regression, interaction, mediation, and stratified analyses. Innate immune activation was observed as a shared BMI-independent pathway linking PCOS and OSA. BMI appeared as a mediator, rather than an effect modifier, in the association between innate immune activation and the two disorders. Disease-specific immune divergence masked by elevated BMI was further observed: neutrophils showed positive associations with PCOS but not OSA, whereas monocytes were positively correlated with OSA but not PCOS. Suggestive genetic signals for EIF2AK2 were detected without robust statistical support from gene-based analyses. We proposed an evolutionary immunological hypothesis for the comorbidity of PCOS and OSA: ancient viral selective pressures might have shaped a hyperreactive innate immune baseline beneficial for ancestral survival, yet such adaptive traits could become maladaptive under modern lifestyles, potentially contributing to chronic low-grade inflammation and increasing PCOS and OSA susceptibility. These findings might clarify the pathological correlation between PCOS and OSA and offer new insights to clinical preventive and therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Acupuncture and related needling in sports-related knee rehabilitation: a narrative review of neurophysiological mechanisms and assessment methods.
papers.abstract: Sports-related knee injuries, including anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture, patellofemoral pain (PFP), meniscal injury, and post-traumatic knee osteoarthritis (KOA), are not only problems of local tissue damage. They can alter joint afferent input, quadriceps activation, cortical control, confidence during return-to-sport, and long-term function. For this reason, knee rehabilitation in athletes need to consider both tissue healing and neurophysiological recovery. Manual acupuncture, electroacupuncture (EA), and trigger point dry needling (DN) have been investigated as adjunctive therapies for knee pain and rehabilitation. Manual acupuncture and EA are needle-based interventions derived from traditional Chinese medicine. DN is included here because of its relevance to musculoskeletal rehabilitation, rather than as a traditional Chinese medicine intervention. Clinical studies suggest possible improvements in pain, swelling, range of motion, self-reported function, and neuromuscular performance. Mechanistic studies also suggest effects on cortical hemodynamics, sensorimotor oscillations, descending pain modulation, spinal excitability, muscle activity, and arthrogenic muscle inhibition (AMI). However, direct evidence specifically in sports-related knee injury populations remains limited. This review discusses evidence from functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), electroencephalography (EEG), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), electromyography (EMG), clinical acupuncture research, and sports rehabilitation. We group the possible mechanisms into cortical intended, corticospinal or spinal-reflexive, and peripheral muscular levels. This framework is intended to guide future research rather than to imply established causality. Given the limited direct evidence currently available in sports-related knee populations, this review is intentionally hypothesis-generating in nature. Its primary value lies in synthesizing indirect evidence from related fields, constructing a testable mechanistic framework, and proposing concrete experimental designs to inform future research.

papers.title: Cybervictimization and psychological burden among internet users aged 15 years and older: online harassment, fraud, and co-victimization.
papers.abstract: Digital victimization is heterogeneous, yet population studies rarely distinguish interpersonal cybervictimization from fraud or determine whether co-occurrence adds psychological burden. We analyzed public-use data from 17,403 Internet users aged ≥15 years in a Canadian population victimization survey. Five-year indicators defined four groups: neither exposure, fraud only, cyberstalking/cyberbullying only, and both; fraud delivery mode was unavailable. The primary outcome was fair/poor self-rated mental health; secondary outcomes were recent medication use to aid sleep, calmness, or depression and current life satisfaction (0-10). Weighted modified Poisson and linear models used all 500 survey bootstrap replicate weights. Core models adjusted for sociodemographic characteristics, religious affiliation, and Internet use; extended models also included conventional victimization, offline stalking, and discrimination. After extended adjustment, fair/poor mental health was more prevalent in the cyber-only group [prevalence ratio (PR) 1.30, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.05-1.62]. The both-exposure estimate was elevated but imprecise (PR 1.38, 95% CI 0.99-1.94), and the fraud-only CI included the null (PR 1.12, 95% CI 0.93-1.36). All exposed groups had lower life satisfaction; medication associations were weaker. Interaction estimates did not establish synergy. The added adversity variables may have multiple temporal roles, so attenuation between models is not a mediation estimate. The released age variable combines ages 15-34, precluding adolescent-specific estimates. Coordinated assessment is a practice implication that requires evaluation.

papers.title: Comparative efficacy of different digital technologies in adults with insomnia: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the efficacy of eight digital interventions for adults with insomnia and compare their relative effects using Bayesian network meta-analysis, so as to provide evidence-based references for digital insomnia management. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were retrieved from six electronic databases up to February 7, 2026. Eligible studies enrolled adult participants with insomnia, with primary outcomes including the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Sleep Onset Latency (SOL), and Wake After Sleep Onset (WASO). Risk of bias was assessed using the RoB 2.0 tool. Intervention hierarchies were obtained using the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA). The GRADE framework for network meta-analysis was applied to rate evidence certainty. Twenty-six RCTs involving 6 353 participants covering eight digital interventions were included. Conventional meta-analysis showed that digital interventions significantly reduced ISI (MD = 3.31, 95%CI 2.48-4.15, P< 0.001, I²= 67%), improved PSQI (MD = 1.52, 95%CI 1.07-1.97, P < 0.001, I² = 0%), and shortened SOL (MD = 12.60, 95%CI 7.66-17.55, P < 0.001, I² = 0%) and WASO (MD = 16.93, 95%CI 8.90-24.96, P < 0.001, I² = 0%). Network meta-analysis suggested that combined digital cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia with wearable devices (DCBT-I+WD) and biofeedback (BF) obtained favourable SUCRA ranks for ISI reduction; BF and digital cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (DCBT-I) ranked highly for PSQI improvement; DCBT-I had the highest SUCRA for SOL reduction; DCBT-I and digital sleep education (DSE) showed relatively good performance for WASO reduction. Different digital technologies can significantly improve various sleep outcomes among adults with insomnia. DCBT-I showed favourable effect estimates. However, data on some digital interventions in some outcomes were mainly based on limited primary studies with sparse direct comparative evidence and thus were highly uncertain and do not allow firm conclusions. Large-sample, multicentre, longitudinal RCTs remain necessary to verify their long-term therapeutic effects.
keywords: digital cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia

papers.title: Temporal dissociation across the eye-brain-muscle cascade delineates a preparation window before muscle activation in subacute stroke.
papers.abstract: Upper-limb motor impairment after stroke is compounded by a disrupted sensorimotor cascade linking visual attention, cortical motor preparation, and peripheral muscle activation. Whether these stages are temporally dissociated in subacute stroke, and whether their timing carries information about the preparation and execution of a reaching action, remains unclear. Thirty subacute stroke survivors and 30 healthy controls performed a full-plane nine-grid reaching task while eye-tracking, electroencephalography (EEG), and surface electromyography (EMG) were recorded synchronously. Three neurophysiological latencies were extracted: first fixation on the target, stimulus-locked lateralized readiness potential (s-LRP) onset, and peripheral muscle activation onset. Compared with controls, patients showed a stepwise delay across the cascade, with delayed visual engagement (616.73 ms vs. 367.86 ms) and delayed peripheral muscle activation (1,080 ms vs. 605 ms) bracketing a cortical preparation window. A random-forest classifier was trained on window-level gaze-timing features, computed separately for each target-presentation and inter-target interval of the task. Under participant-level leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, it achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.973 (95% CI 0.958-0.984) and an accuracy of 0.918, numerically the highest among the five classifiers compared. These findings describe a quantifiable temporal organization of the sensorimotor cascade in the subacute stage of stroke and indicate that gaze timing carries discriminative information about the occurrence of an instructed reaching action. They establish a descriptive, testable framework rather than a demonstrated clinical benefit. Validation in chronic stroke and across independent samples is further required.

papers.title: Protocol-aware dual-view single-channel EEG sleep staging with improved N1 discrimination on public sleep-EDF and SHHS benchmarks.
papers.abstract: To develop and evaluate DualViewSeqSleepNet, a protocol-aware single-channel EEG model for automatic sleep staging under reproducible public benchmark settings. The model integrates raw-waveform and spectral encoders, gated epoch-level fusion, lightweight bidirectional cross-epoch aggregation, and an auxiliary loss targeting Wake-N1 and N1-N2 transitions. Primary testing used the exact Sleep-EDF SC-subset protocol of SeriesSleepNet. Secondary no-retuning evaluation used SHHS-1 healthy C4-A1 data. On Sleep-EDF, DualViewSeqSleepNet achieved macro-F1 0.821, accuracy 0.869, and Cohen's kappa 0.808, exceeding the SeriesSleepNet anchor and improving N1 F1 from 0.506 to 0.535. On SHHS-1, it reached macro-F1 0.791 and accuracy 0.854 without architecture-family retuning. Ablation and robustness analyses supported the contributions of dual-view fusion, cross-epoch aggregation, and N1-aware supervision. DualViewSeqSleepNet provides a modest, protocol-aligned improvement for public single-channel sleep staging, especially near Wake-N1-N2 boundaries, but does not establish external clinical validation or autonomous deployment readiness.

papers.title: Integrated rehabilitation for post-stroke anxiety: a prospective, multicenter, randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Post-stroke anxiety (PSA) affects approximately one-quarter of stroke survivors and impedes functional recovery, yet pharmacological options remain limited by inconsistent efficacy and absent standardized guidelines. This study evaluated an integrated rehabilitation program combining repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), acupuncture, and Chinese herbal medicine for PSA. In this multicenter randomized controlled trial, 188 participants with mild-to-moderate PSA were randomized 1:1 to standard care (pharmacotherapy, general care, and exercise therapy) or integrated rehabilitation (standard care plus rTMS, acupuncture, and Chinese herbal medicine) for 4 weeks, with an 8-week follow-up. The primary outcome was the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A). Secondary outcomes included the Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS), Activities of Daily Living (ADL), Instrumental Activities of Daily Living (IADL), Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), Fugl-Meyer Assessment (FMA), and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Analyses followed an intention-to-treat framework. The integrated rehabilitation group showed significantly greater reductions in HAM-A scores at Week 4 than controls (between-group difference, 2.49 points; 95% CI, 1.50 to 3.48; p <0.01), and this treatment benefit was maintained at week 12 (p<0.01). In supportive analyses of the secondary outcomes, Holm-adjusted group × time interactions remained significant for PSQI, MoCA, upper-extremity motor function, ADL, and SAS scores (all adjusted p<0.05), but not for lower-extremity motor function or IADL. The integrated rehabilitation program improved the primary anxiety outcome and provided supportive evidence of broader clinical benefits in sleep quality, cognition, and upper-extremity motor function, together with distinct patterns of functional change in ADL and IADL. Overall, these findings support further consideration of this integrated approach as an adjunct to pharmacotherapy for PSA. Biological mechanisms and contributions of individual intervention components remain undetermined. Further mechanistic investigations incorporating biological measures would help clarify the underlying mechanisms. https://clinicaltrials.gov/, identifier NCT05147077.

papers.title: Construction of a nomogram prediction model for symptom residue after tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy in children with obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome based on lasso-logistic regression analysis.
papers.abstract: To identify the factors associated with residual symptoms after adenotonsillectomy in children with obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS) using LASSO-logistic regression, and to construct a nomogram prediction model. A total of 324 children with OSAHS treated at our hospital from January 2023 to March 2024 were enrolled and randomly divided into a training cohort (n = 227) and an internal validation cohort (n = 97) at a ratio of 7:3. According to the 1-year follow-up results, the training cohort was further divided into a recovery group and a residual symptom group. In addition, 175 children with OSAHS treated at our hospital from April 2024 to January 2025 were included as an external validation cohort. LASSO-logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of postoperative residual symptoms. A nomogram model was then established and evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, calibration curves, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Compared with the recovery group, children in the residual symptom group were younger and had higher proportions of males, BMI > the 95th percentile, family history of OSAHS, asthma, rhinitis, >8 spontaneous awakenings per hour before surgery, AHI > 18 events/h before surgery, as well as higher preoperative mYPAS scores and postoperative Wong-Baker scores (all P < 0.05). LASSO-logistic regression identified sex, BMI, asthma, rhinitis, number of spontaneous awakenings before surgery, and preoperative AHI as independent predictors (all P < 0.05). The AUC values of the nomogram in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts were 0.874, 0.851, and 0.850, respectively. Calibration curves showed good agreement between predicted and observed outcomes, and DCA demonstrated favorable clinical utility. The nomogram showed good predictive performance and may help assess the risk of residual symptoms after adenotonsillectomy in children with OSAHS.

papers.title: Perioperative esketamine is associated with attenuated sleep deprivation-related cognitive dysfunction: a retrospective biomarker cohort study of the ferroptosis-neuroinflammation axis.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation is common in older surgical patients and may increase vulnerability to postoperative neurocognitive dysfunction through oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and regulated cell-death pathways. Experimental studies increasingly implicate hippocampal ferroptosis, particularly disruption of the SLC7A11-GSH-GPX4 defense axis, in sleep-deprivation-related cognitive injury. Esketamine has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, but whether its perioperative neurocognitive benefit is associated with a ferroptosis-related molecular phenotype in clinical patients remains uncertain. We conducted a retrospective biomarker cohort study of 398 adults aged 60-80 years who underwent elective major non-cardiac surgery between January 2022 and December 2025. Patients were classified according to preoperative sleep deprivation (total sleep time <4 h and sleep efficiency <70% during the night before surgery) and perioperative esketamine exposure, generating four groups: NSD-C, NSD-E, SD-C, and SD-E. The primary outcome was early postoperative cognitive decline on postoperative day (POD) 7, defined by a ≥1-SD deterioration in a composite neuropsychological Z score. In a biomarker subcohort, plasma 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE), malondialdehyde (MDA), glutathione (GSH), glutathione peroxidase activity, inflammatory cytokines, neuronal injury markers, and PBMC expression of GPX4, SLC7A11, and ACSL4 were analyzed. Confounding was addressed using multivariable models and inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting. Bootstrap mediation models examined a ferroptosis-related redox score and IL-6 as candidate mediators. In the cohort, cognitive decline occurred in 32.5% of sleep-deprived patients without esketamine and 17.7% of sleep-deprived patients exposed to esketamine. After adjustment, esketamine exposure in the sleep-deprivation subgroup was associated with lower odds of cognitive decline (adjusted OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.26-0.92). Sleep deprivation was associated with higher 4-HNE, MDA, ACSL4, IL-6, TNF-α, and NSE and lower GSH, GPX activity, GPX4, and SLC7A11; these abnormalities were attenuated in the esketamine-exposed group. The exploratory ferroptosis-related redox score was independently associated with cognitive decline. Under the specified exploratory mediation model, the estimated total mediated proportion was 54%; this model-based decomposition does not establish causal biological mediation. Perioperative esketamine was associated with less pronounced early postoperative cognitive decline in sleep-deprived patients and a less pronounced peripheral ferroptosis-related/inflammatory phenotype.
papers.journal: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology

papers.title: Potential symptom management targets following transarterial chemoembolization in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma: a network analysis and computer-simulation study.
papers.abstract: Potential symptom intervention targets in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) after transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) remain poorly understood. Symptom network analysis combined with computer-simulated interventions may help identify priority targets for symptom management. To examine symptom associations and explore potential symptom management targets among patients with HCC following TACE. A cross-sectional study included 312 patients with HCC. Symptoms were assessed 24-48 h after TACE using the Chinese versions of the M. D. Anderson Symptom Inventory and the primary liver cancer-specific symptom module. A Gaussian graphical model was used to examine symptom associations, while an Ising model and NodeIdentifyR algorithm were used to explore simulated symptom perturbations. Fatigue (86.5%), disturbed sleep (83.7%), and lack of appetite (75.0%) were the most prevalent symptoms. Nausea showed the highest estimated strength centrality. Hypothetical alleviation of dry mouth produced the largest model-predicted decrease in the mean number of active symptoms, whereas hypothetical aggravation of fever produced the largest increase. Nausea was the most connected symptom according to estimated strength centrality. Dry mouth and fever showed the largest model-predicted responses to alleviating and aggravating threshold perturbations, respectively. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation; they do not establish clinical treatment effects.

papers.title: Nocturnal Sweating in Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Systematic Review and Exploratory Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is commonly associated with symptoms such as snoring and daytime sleepiness, while atypical manifestations including nocturnal sweating remain less clearly understood. The current systematic review aimed to evaluate the relationship between nocturnal sweating and OSA and to explore possible physiological mechanisms underlying this association. A systematic search identified 10 relevant studies including observational, physiological, and treatment-response investigations. The included studies varied substantially in design, patient characteristics, and methods of assessing nocturnal sweating. Early studies mainly described nocturnal sweating as a nonspecific symptom among OSA patients and failed to demonstrate consistent associations with conventional severity indices such as the apnea-hypopnea index. However, more recent studies have suggested that nocturnal sweating may be associated with hypoxemic burden, rapid eye movement (REM)-related respiratory worsening, sleep fragmentation, and sympathetic nervous system activation rather than respiratory event frequency alone. Physiological studies have demonstrated improvement in sweating after continuous or automatic positive airway pressure therapy, supporting a reversible autonomic mechanism. An exploratory meta-analysis of three comparative studies showed a non-significant increase in nocturnal sweating among OSA patients (odds ratio [OR] = 1.85; 95%CI: 0.87-3.92; I 2 = 91.7%). After exclusion of one study involving untreated moderate-to-severe OSA patients, heterogeneity decreased but the association remained non-significant (OR = 1.31; 95%CI: 0.76-2.23; I 2 = 64.7%). Overall, nocturnal sweating does not appear to represent a specific diagnostic marker of OSA itself, but it may reflect physiological consequences of untreated or severe disease in susceptible individuals.

papers.title: Effects of Circadian Disruption and Chronotype on Postural Stability During Quiet Stance.
papers.abstract: Postural control is fundamental for daily activities and is known to be sensitive to disruptions of the circadian system. The present study investigated how individual circadian alignment influences postural stability in healthy adults. In total, 39 participants wore actigraphs for 2 weeks to obtain circadian regularity and misalignment parameters: composite phase deviation (CPD), interdaily stability (IS), and intradaily variability (IV). Chronotype was assessed from corrected midsleep time on free days. Postural stability was evaluated through center of pressure (COP) trajectories recorded while the participant stood on a force platform under different sensory conditions. Postural dynamics were analyzed using both linear sway measures and recurrence quantification analysis, with particular focus on laminarity (LAM) and trapping time (TT) as indicators of postural control stability and adaptability. Higher circadian disruption, reflected by increased CPD and reduced IS, was associated with greater postural instability, characterized by increased sway magnitude and higher values of LAM and TT, suggesting more intermittent and less adaptive postural control strategies. Additionally, individuals with later chronotypes exhibited poorer postural stability compared with those with earlier chronotypes. Therefore, these findings indicate that circadian disruption is associated with alterations in postural control dynamics, potentially reducing the adaptability of the postural system. Even in healthy adults, irregular sleep-wake patterns may place the sensorimotor system in a suboptimal state, increasing vulnerability to balance impairments.

papers.title: Ultrasound-Measured Posterior Neck-Fold Thickness and Tongue-Base Thickness as Anatomical Markers in Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Pilot Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) affects nearly 1 billion adults globally. Polysomnography (PSG) is the diagnostic gold standard, but it is resource-intensive. Ultrasound assessment of posterior cervical soft tissue is underexplored. To evaluate the correlations involving ultrasound-measured posterior neck-fold thickness (PNFT) and tongue-base thickness (TBT) with PSG severity indices in OSA patients. We conducted a prospective study of 77 adults with PSG-confirmed OSA. Bedside ultrasound assessed PNFT and TBT. Neck circumference (NC) and indices (apnea-hypopnea index [AHI], oxygen desaturation index [ODI], and lowest oxygen saturation [LSAT]) were recorded. In total, 38 patients had mild-to-moderate OSA, and 39, severe OSA. The NC was larger in the severe group compared to the mild-to-moderate group (41.9 versus 38.4 cm respectively; p < 0.001). Neither the PNFT (mild-to-moderate group: 9.3; severe group: 10.2 mm; p = 0.184) nor the TBT (mild-to-moderate group: 65.9; severe group: 67.5 mm; p = 0.167) differed significantly between the groups; the small observed effect size (Cohen's d = 0.31 for TBT) reflects limited precision with this sample size rather than confirmatory evidence against a true difference. The PNFT correlated weakly with the AHI (r = 0.238; p = 0.037) and LSAT (r = -0.228; p = 0.048). The TBT showed a moderate correlation with the LSAT (r = -0.424; p < 0.001) and a weak correlation with the ODI (r = 0.238; p = 0.038). Except for the TBT-LSAT association, none of these ultrasound correlations remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. The TBT showed a modest, sex-independent association with the LSAT, whereas PNFT's associations with OSA severity were largely attributable to sex rather than an independent anatomical effect.

papers.title: Metrics Reflecting Cumulative Exposure to Nocturnal Hypoxia Demonstrate Promising Performance in Distinguishing between Moderate and Severe Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
papers.abstract: The apnea-hypopnea index is traditionally used to classify the severity of obstructive sleep apnea; however, it does not fully capture the cumulative physiological impact of nocturnal hypoxia. Metrics that quantify integrated hypoxic exposure may provide a more accurate characterization of disease severity. The current study compared the independent association and discriminative performance of hypoxic burden, cumulative time with peripheral oxygen saturation below 90%, and oxygen desaturation frequency in distinguishing between moderate and severe obstructive sleep apnea. In total, 30 patients with moderate or severe disease were evaluated using actigraphy combined with continuous nocturnal oximetry. Separate logistic regression models adjusted for body mass index were developed. Hypoxic burden and cumulative time with peripheral oxygen saturation below 90% remained independently associated with severe disease, with odds ratios of 1.35 (95%CI: 1.05-1.75; p = 0.021) and 2.46 (95%CI: 1.03-5.90; p = 0.043) respectively, whereas desaturation frequency was not significant after adjustment (odds ratio: 1.90; 95%CI: 0.97-3.73; p = 0.061). The model including cumulative time with peripheral oxygen saturation below 90% yielded an area under the curve of 0.86 (95%CI: 0.728-0.996), while the models including hypoxic burden and desaturation frequency yielded values regarding the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of 0.84 (95%CI: 0.698-0.989) and 0.78 (95%CI: 0.618-0.954) respectively. These findings suggest good discriminative performance of metrics reflecting cumulative nocturnal hypoxic exposure; however, formal comparisons between the ROC curves were not performed. Metrics reflecting cumulative exposure to nocturnal hypoxia demonstrated promising performance in distinguishing between moderate and severe disease, and they may contribute to risk stratification in obstructive sleep apnea.

papers.title: Actimetry-Derived Sleep and Circadian Parameters in a Population-Based Sample from São Paulo: Findings from the EPISONO Cohort.
papers.abstract: To set benchmarks for sleep estimates and for parameters of rest-activity, light exposure, and skin temperature rhythms in a cohort from São Paulo. The present study used data from the 4th edition of the São Paulo Epidemiologic Sleep Study (Estudo Epidemiológico do Sono da cidade de São Paulo, EPISONO, in Portuguese), conducted between 2018 and 2019 ( N = 769). A subset of 404 participants (60% female; mean age: 49.42 ± 14.90 years) was selected based on standardized 7-day records (5 weekdays and 2 free days). Sleep estimates, cosine-based and nonparametric parameters, were extracted and added as dependent variables in generalized linear models to investigate the effects of age, sex, body mass index, socioeconomic status, season of data collection and daylight-saving time on it. Participants aged 40 years or older had earlier sleep, circadian and light exposure timing, and reduced activity levels and amplitude. Females slept longer than males and exhibited a more stable and less fragmented rest-activity rhythm but displayed impaired patterns of exposure to light. Lower socioeconomic status was associated with poorer sleep quality yet less disrupted rhythms. Obesity was correlated with greater instability in the rest-activity rhythm. Seasonal differences revealed that sleep was shorter and later in the spring compared with winter. Our results established reference values for actimetry parameters in the largest city in Latin America and can be applied to similar urban populations. They also highlight vulnerable subgroups with impaired sleep and circadian patterns in this understudied context. These findings can inform public health policies and guide the design of personalized interventions.

papers.title: Validation of the Korean Version of the Biphasic Sleep Scale (BiSS) and Its Associations with Insomnia and Sleep-Related Cognition.
papers.abstract: The present study aimed to assess the psychometric properties of the Korean version of the Biphasic Sleep Scale (BiSS), including its factor structure, reliability, and validity, in a Korean population. An online survey was applied to the general population. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses were used to explore whether the three-factor model of the BiSS was retained in the Korean context. Convergent validity was compared with the Insomnia Severity Index, the 9-Item Patient Health Questionnaire, the Dysfunctional Beliefs and Attitudes about Sleep-6, and the Adaptive Cognition and Behaviors about Sleep-6 scales. The Korean BiSS was clustered into four factors: reason, consequences, nighttime sleep disturbance, and positive aspects. The confirmatory factor analysis showed that the four-factor model fit the data better than the original three-factor model. The four-factor model showed an acceptable fit (comparative fit index [CFI] =0.903; Tucker-Lewis index [TLI] = 0.881; root-mean-square error of approximation [RMSEA] = 0.093; and standardized root-mean-square residual [SRMR] = 0.053), while the three-factor model showed a poorer fit (CFI = 0.772; TLI = 0.730; RMSEA = 0.140; SRMR = 0.104). Internal consistency reliability was high, with a McDonald's omega of 0.914 in the four-factor model. The total BiSS score was inversely correlated with the desired bedtime and positively correlated with insomnia severity (r = 0.12) and dysfunctional beliefs about sleep (r = 0.21). In the regression analysis, the DBAS-6 was the only significant variable, but the model only explained a small proportion of the variance (adjusted R 2 = 0.05). The four-factor model of the Korean BiSS is a reliable and valid measure for assessing people's perceptions, preferences, and habits related to biphasic sleep, which involves nighttime sleep and daytime naps.

papers.title: Directional brain-heart interaction during cognitive workload: a permutation conditional mutual information approach.
papers.abstract: The functional interaction between the central nervous system and autonomic cardiovascular regulation, commonly referred to as Brain-Heart Interaction (BHI), has gained increasing attention in neurology and psychology through the joint analysis of Electroencephalography (EEG) and Electrocardiography (ECG) signals. However, the nonlinear and time-varying nature of EEG and ECG signals requires approaches that can capture directional interactions between physiological systems. In this study, we investigated the use of Permutation Conditional Mutual Information (PCMI) for the characterization of directional BHI. First, the method was evaluated on synthetically generated coupled time series to assess its ability to detect the dominant direction of interaction. Next, PCMI was applied to simultaneous EEG and ECG recordings acquired during baseline and mental arithmetic tasks from a cohort of 36 subjects. The results show that BHI complexity increases during mental arithmetic tasks compared with baseline, supporting the role of cognitive workload in modulating brain-heart dynamics. These changes primarily involved anterior and posterior scalp regions, and affected both vagal- and sympathovagal-related HRV components. These findings demonstrate that PCMI provides a framework for studying directional BHI during cognitive tasks, and highlight its potential translational value for investigating broader brain-body interactions.

papers.title: Electrical Vestibular Stimulation in Primary and Comorbid Insomnia: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is a common disorder associated with impaired daytime functioning and psychiatric comorbidities such as anxiety and depression. Electrical vestibular nerve stimulation (VeNS) has emerged as a potential nonpharmacological treatment due to the vestibular system's role in sleep regulation. To evaluate the safety and efficacy of VeNS versus sham stimulation in reducing insomnia severity, improving sleep quality and quality of life, and alleviating anxiety symptoms in adults with primary or psychiatric comorbid insomnia. In total, 6 databases were systematically searched from inception to September 2025, following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Randomized sham-controlled trials evaluating VeNS for insomnia were included. Random-effects models estimated mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and heterogeneity was assessed using I 2 . Of the 5 studies included, three were on primary insomnia (n = 310) and 2, on psychiatric comorbid insomnia (n = 120). The use of VeNS significantly reduced insomnia severity index scores in both primary (mean difference [MD]: -3.42; 95%CI: -6.58 to -0.26) and psychiatric comorbid (MD: -5.51; 95%CI: -8.49 to -2.52) cases. Greater benefits were observed in younger adults. While this treatment did not significantly improve global sleep quality, it did improve quality-of-life domains including vitality, mental health, and physical functioning. Anxiety symptoms were also significantly reduced. Adverse events were mild and infrequent, with no consistent device-related serious events reported. The use of VeNS may reduce insomnia severity and anxiety with good tolerability. However, evidence is limited by small sample sizes and substantial heterogeneity. Larger, high-quality, randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these findings.

papers.title: Cheek Characteristics and Their Relationship with Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
papers.abstract: To investigate whether cheek appearance, posture, mobility, and pressure are associated with the presence and severity of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in adults. Te currents cross-sectional study included 100 adults aged 18 to 59 years, classified as controls or as having mild, moderate, or severe OSA based on type-I polysomnography. Cheek appearance/posture and mobility were assessed using the Expanded Protocol of Orofacial Myofunctional Evaluation with Scores, and cheek pressure was measured using the Iowa Oral Performance Instrument (model 2.2; IOPI Medical LLC). Descriptive statistics, Spearman's correlation tests, Mann-Whitney tests, and multiple linear regression were performed at a significance level of 5%. The apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) was positively correlated with the body mass index (BMI) and negatively correlated with cheek appearance/posture scores, whereas cheek mobility and cheek pressure were not significantly correlated with the AHI. Across OSA severity groups, cheek appearance/posture scores differed significantly: individuals with moderate and severe OSA had lower scores than the controls. No significant between-group differences were observed for cheek mobility or pressure. In the multivariable analyses, the BMI was the only variable independently associated with the AHI. Neither cheek appearance/posture nor cheek mobility remained independently associated with the AHI after adjustment for age, sex, and BMI, and cheek pressure was also not independently associated with the AHI in the secondary model. Cheek appearance/posture was associated with OSA severity in the unadjusted analyses, but it did not remain independently associated with the AHI after adjustment for age, sex, and BMI. Cheek mobility and pressure showed limited associations with OSA severity.

papers.title: Associations of Sleep Patterns With Semen Quality in Sperm Donors: Insights From Untargeted Metabolomics.
papers.abstract: Sleep problems are common but their associations with semen quality remain controversial. To investigate individual and interactive associations of sleep duration and sleep quality with semen quality. This prospective cohort included 3474 sperm donor applicants, from whom 11,427 semen samples were collected. The Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) was employed to assess sleep quality. Semen analysis was performed according to the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations. Semen quality parameters were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. Potential nonlinear relationships were explored using restricted cubic splines and interaction analyses were conducted to evaluate the modifying effect of sleep quality on the relationship of nighttime sleep duration with semen quality. Compared with those sleeping 7-9 h/day, men with total sleep duration < 7 h/day or nighttime sleep duration < 7 h/day had reduced sperm concentration, total sperm count, and progressive and total motility. Likewise, men with PSQI > 5 had lower levels of these semen parameters than those with PSQI ≤ 5. Dose-response analyses demonstrated inverted U-shaped relationships for sleep duration, whereas PSQI scores were linearly and negatively associated with sperm concentration and motility. After FDR correction, sleep quality significantly modified the relationships between nighttime sleep duration and sperm concentration, but not for progressive or total motility. Mediation analysis conducted in a subset of 87 participants who underwent metabolomics analyses suggested that dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate, isovaleryl-L-carnitine, and cytarabine may serve as potential mediators. Short sleep duration and poor sleep quality were associated with lower semen quality, and the latter might modify the association between sleep duration and semen quality. The three metabolites may serve as potential mediators, though causal inference is limited by the observational design and self-reported sleep data.

papers.title: Hidden Drowsiness in Wakefulness: Differences in Resting-State EEG Profiles in Natural Short Sleepers Versus Recommended Length Sleepers.
papers.abstract: Chronic insufficient sleep affects cardiovascular, endocrine, immune and nervous systems and is linked to cognitive decline and increased mortality. Among habitual short sleepers, a subgroup known as natural short sleepers (NSS) report sleeping ≤ 6 h per night without experiencing subjective daytime dysfunction. However, discrepancies between subjective and objective markers of alertness raise questions about their true cognitive state. NSS have been described as high in behavioural activation, a phenotype overlapping with ADHD and mania in which dysregulation of resting-state brain arousal has been well documented. Despite these parallels, few studies have investigated the neurophysiological features of NSS. The current study examined resting-state EEG in NSS and recommended-length sleepers (RLS) during eyes-open conditions. Results showed that NSS exhibited significantly higher global alpha power and regionally steeper aperiodic exponents, particularly in occipital areas, both markers of increased drowsiness. Although global exponent values did not differ significantly, a significant Group × Region interaction was observed and NSS showed a trend toward increasing aperiodic exponents over time, suggesting less stable wakefulness under low-stimulation conditions. These findings point to subtle neurophysiological differences in NSS, raising the possibility that their perceived resilience to short sleep may mask underlying drowsiness.

papers.title: Implementation, Reach, and Safety of Physical Activity Interventions for Autistic Adults: A Scoping Review.
papers.abstract: Despite the known benefits of physical activity-such as better sleep, increased social connection, and reduced psychological distress-autistic adults often do not meet recommended levels. As physical and psychological conditions often co-occur with autism, increasing physical activity represents a potential avenue for improved health and well-being outcomes. Physical activity research to date has primarily focused on autistic children and adolescents. The aim of this study was to understand the implementation, reach, and safety of physical activity programs for autistic adults. We conducted a scoping review. Reported according to PRISMA-ScR guidelines, our review included studies implementing physical activity interventions in autistic people aged ≥18 years. We searched six databases to June 2024 with keywords, MeSH headings and derivatives relating to autism and physical activity. We extracted data using a standardized template, applying a descriptive analytical approach to map data to categories associated with the review's aim. Nine studies involving 148 autistic adults (108 male; aged 19-34 years) met inclusion criteria. Physical activity interventions implemented included aerobic exercise, walking or jogging, strength training, motor skills training, soccer, and exer-gaming. Trained instructors, exercise or health professionals, students, coaches, teaching assistants, or residential staff supervised programs conducted in home, school, university, or community settings. Strategies used to support implementation were incorporating appropriate adaptations and scaffolding, using social support strategies and facilitating self-determination. Elements of reach were described variably among the included studies. Reasons for reduced reach and nonparticipation included lack of interest, scheduling, and medical and personal issues. Safety strategies included conducting pre-exercise medical screening and providing physical and psychological training for support people. Safe implementation of physical activity among autistic adults is possible with support. However, there is a lack of research addressing physical activity among autistic women and those with complex needs. Why is this an important issue?: Autistic adults have high rates of physical inactivity, and many do not meet physical activity guidelines promoted by the World Health Organization. The benefits of physical activity include improved sleep, increased social interactions, and reduced psychological distress. Participation in physical activity is important for autistic adults who have a propensity to sleep poorly, be socially isolated, and have a high likelihood of mental health issues.What was the purpose of the review?: In this scoping review, we sought to identify and describe what is known about physical activity interventions for autistic adults and understand how the interventions worked in practice, who took part, and the safety of these interventions.What did the authors do to review the literature?: Following published guidelines for conducting scoping reviews, we identified and screened peer-reviewed articles for studies that investigated a physical activity intervention involving autistic adults. We extracted information from each study to better understand how the intervention was carried out, who took part and the reasons for this, and the safety of the interventions, including any measures to ensure safe participation.What studies did the authors find?: We identified nine studies describing physical activity interventions for autistic adults. Most participants were male, and all studies were done in high-income countries. The types of physical activity carried out were weight and aerobic training, walking and jogging programs, motor skill development, soccer, swimming and "exer-gaming" (i.e., active video games). These activities were completed either in small groups or one-to-one and were supervised by a trained person. Strategies to support participation included logistical support, orientation and specialist support, and motivation and peer support. Support strategies were used to adapt and give structure to the activity to meet the needs of individuals. Only one study gave reasons for people not taking part, which included a lack of interest, scheduling, and personal issues. Preexisting health conditions and complexity of needs excluded some autistic adults from taking part. Safety strategies included pre-exercise screening, having cardiopulmonary resuscitation-trained supervisors and physical and psychological training for support people. No studies reported adverse events because of participation in physical activity.In summary, what did those studies show?: Having support in place, making adaptations, and having a structure that meets an individual's needs and preferences may facilitate uptake of physical activity among autistic adults.What are the remaining gaps in the literature?: Understanding the reasons for low or nonparticipation needs further exploration. There remains a need to better understand physical activity from the perspective of autistic women and among autistic individuals with complex needs and those living in low-income countries.Based on this review, what do the authors recommend?: Understanding the needs of all autistic adults is important to facilitate their uptake and inclusion in a variety of physical activities regardless of the setting. Autistic individuals need to be included in the design of physical activity programs to ensure their needs and preferences are met. Further, there is a need for physical activity programs that can translate to low socioeconomic environments.
